etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Early Modern English conferre, from Middle French conférer, from Old French conferer, from Latin cōnferō. Compare Dutch confereren (“to confer”), German konferieren (“to confer”), Danish konferere (“to confer”), Swedish konferera (“to confer”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To grant as a possession; to bestow. [from 16th c.]

quote.text: Nor shall I count in hainous to enjoyThe public marks of honour and reward Conferr'd upon me […]

quote.citation: 1850, T. S. Arthur, “Deacon Smith and his Violin”, in Sketches of Life and Character‎[1], Philadelphia: J. W. Bradley, →OCLC, page 76:
quote.text: Abel tried to refuse the honor thus unexpectedly conferred upon him, but it was no use. He had been made a deacon, and a deacon he must remain.
The special immunities that are conferred on MPs were framed with the essential purpose of allowing them to speak freely in parliament.

quote.citation: 2014, James Lambert, “Diachronic stability in Indian English lexis”, in World Englishes, page 114:
quote.text: The mere existence of a dictionary of a certain variety of English does not automatically confer acceptance of that variety.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To talk together, to consult, discuss; to deliberate. [from 16th c.]

quote.text: Local buttons popped when Henry Kissinger visited Little Rock last month to confer with Fulbright on the Middle East oil talks.
The Newe Testament ... Conferred diligently with the Greke, and best approued translations.

quote.citation: 1624, Democritus Junior [pseudonym; Robert Burton], The Anatomy of Melancholy: […], 2nd edition, Oxford, Oxfordshire:  […]  John Lichfield and James Short, for Henry Cripps, →OCLC, partition II, section 3, member 1, subsection i:
quote.text: Confer thine estate with others […]. Be content and rest satisfied, for thou art well in respect to others […].

quote.citation: 1661, Robert Boyle, The Second Essay, of Unsucceeding Experiments:
quote.text: If we confer these observations with others of the like nature, we may find cause to rectify the general opinion.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, transitive) To bring together; to collect, gather. [16th–17th c.]

quote.text: The closeness and compactness of the parts resting together doth much confer to the strength of the union.
